The bicycle had been leaning against the Hadleys' trash cans for two days with a sign taped to the seat that said FREE, and on the third morning Nell wheeled it home. It was a green three-speed, older than her parents, with a rusted chain and a back wheel that rubbed against the frame once on every turn.

That night she made a list at the kitchen table: new chain, new tires, new cables, new brakes, new seat, new wheels if the old ones were bent. She looked up every price. The total came to a hundred and sixty dollars, which was nearly all she had saved.

Mr. Ostrowski next door, who had once kept the bicycles running for a delivery company, read the list over the fence the next afternoon and handed it back. "Take it apart first," he said. "Then buy what it needs."

That seemed to Nell like a slow way of reaching the same total. But she borrowed his wrenches, spread an old bedsheet on the garage floor, and laid each part on the sheet in the order it came off, so that she would know how to put it back. The chain soaked overnight in a coffee can of degreaser and came out black but whole. The seat, under a crust of dirt, was cracked leather that oiled up dark and soft. The tires were worn but sound, though the tubes inside them had rotted, and the brakes needed only new pads.

The back wheel was the hard part. Mr. Ostrowski showed her how to true it: tighten a spoke on one side, loosen its neighbor on the other, a quarter turn at a time, never more. She fastened a plastic zip tie to the frame so that its tail just touched the rim, and spun the wheel, and listened. Where the rim bent toward it, the tail ticked. She turned the spoke wrench a quarter turn and spun again.

It took four evenings. On the first she turned a spoke a full half turn because she was tired of waiting, and the tick moved to the other side of the wheel and grew louder. She undid it and went back to quarters.

On the fifth evening the wheel spun past the zip tie in silence. She bought two tubes, two brake pads, and a set of cables, and the receipt came to twenty-six dollars.

She rode the bicycle down the block and back while Mr. Ostrowski watched from his porch. Then she went into the garage, took the first list off the workbench, and folded it into a small, tight square. She wedged it under the short leg of the workbench, which had always rocked a little, and it stopped.

The fog came up from the river in the night
and by six it had taken the town apart.
The water tower is gone. The church is gone.
The far side of Elm Street is only a rumor.

I walk to the bus inside a small gray room
that moves when I move, ten steps wide,
and things arrive in it one at a time:
a mailbox, a hydrant, a dog on a long leash,

then the woman holding the leash, last of all,
as if she had been sent along afterward.
Sounds come closer than the things that make them.
A screen door slaps somewhere I cannot place.

A car goes by with its headlights on,
two pale coins that brighten, then a hiss,
then the red of its taillights folding back
into the wall of the room I carry.

At the corner I count the houses by their porch lights
and come up one short, and stand there counting again,
and the missing house steps out of the gray
exactly where it has stood for forty years.

By eight the sun is a white plate in it.
The gray goes thin and then goes thinner,
and the water tower comes back on its long legs,
and the church, and the far side of Elm Street,

each where I left it, and smaller than I thought,
the way a word looks strange when you say it
twenty times, and then looks plain again.
The bus comes. I get on. The windows are clear.

My uncle Desmond drove a city bus for thirty years, and on his breaks, parked at the end of the line, he knitted. He kept the yarn in a canvas bag under the driver's seat. The winter I was twelve, I stayed with him in the evenings while my parents worked late, and one night I asked him to teach me.

He gave me a pair of wooden needles and a ball of gray wool he called practice yarn. "We'll make a scarf," he said. "Plain stitch, every row. Count as you go." He cast on twenty stitches for me, looping the yarn over the needle so quickly that I could see nothing but his thumb moving, and then he slowed down and did the next row one stitch at a time.

The first week went badly. My stitches were so tight that I had to force the needle through them, and some rows came out with twenty-one stitches and some with nineteen. Each time, Desmond held the scarf up to the lamp, found the place where the count went wrong, and slid the needle out. Then he tugged the yarn, and three evenings of rows came apart into a crinkled heap in my lap.

"You can fix it there," he said, pointing at the stitch. "Or you can carry it the whole length of the scarf."

I told him a single stitch was too small for anyone to see. He said that was true for about six inches. Past that, the count would keep wandering, and the scarf would come out wider at one end than the other, with edges that went in and out like a coastline.

So I counted. I counted out loud at first, and then under my breath, and by February I was counting without noticing it, the way you stop hearing your own footsteps. My stitches loosened. The scarf grew to the length of my arm, then to the length of the couch, with edges that ran straight from end to end.

When it was finished, Desmond tied on the fringe himself and wore the scarf to work the next morning. He wore it for eleven winters, until the gray had worn thin at the neck.

I knit most evenings now. Last month my daughter asked me to teach her, and I cast on twenty stitches, quickly, and then slowed down. On her third evening she held up a row with twenty-two stitches and asked if it mattered. I found the place, slid the needle out, and watched her face as the rows came apart.

In most towns, the center of downtown is given over to a single use. Of the space between the shop windows on Main Street, perhaps three quarters belongs to cars, moving or parked, and the rest is a pair of sidewalks just wide enough for two people to pass. We are so used to this arrangement that it looks like the natural shape of a street rather than a choice someone made.

It was a choice, and it can be made differently. A number of towns in Europe and North America have closed a few central blocks to cars, keeping them open to people on foot and on bicycles, with deliveries allowed in the early morning.

The usual objection comes from the people with the most at stake: the shop owners. Their customers drive, they say, and a customer who cannot park near the door will shop somewhere else. The concern deserves a serious answer, because a downtown of empty storefronts would be worse than the one we have.

Part of the answer is that shop owners may be guessing wrong about their own customers. When researchers in several cities have asked shoppers how they arrived, the share who came by car has often turned out smaller than the shop owners estimated. Some studies have also found that people who walk or ride the bus tend to spend less on each visit but come more often.

Until the spring of 1871, the only light on the streets of Wexley Falls after dark was whatever spilled from windows and the lanterns people carried. That April the town council voted to buy twenty kerosene lamps on cast-iron posts and to hire a lamplighter at eight dollars a month. To pay for them, every household in town would owe a lamp tax of fifty cents a year.

The lamps arrived by rail in June and went up along Front Street, from the depot to the bridge, where the stores and the two hotels stood. The lamplighter was Elias Dorn, nineteen, who walked the street each evening at dusk with a short ladder over his shoulder and a can of kerosene, cleaning each glass chimney, trimming each wick, and lighting it. At midnight he walked the street again and put them out.

To keep the cost down, the council adopted what it called a moon schedule. On the nights nearest the full moon, the lamps would stay dark, since the moon would light the street for free. The schedule was printed in the Wexley Falls Gazette each month, and it saved roughly a fifth of the kerosene.

The schedule did not account for clouds. On an overcast night in October, at the full moon, the town doctor drove his buggy down Front Street in near-total darkness, missed the turn onto the bridge, and put one wheel into the ditch. He was unhurt, but he wrote to the Gazette that the council had arranged to light the town on the nights it needed light least.

Meanwhile, the families of Mill Row, across the river, had paid their fifty cents like everyone else, and Mill Row had no lamps at all. In November forty-one of its households signed a petition asking why they should pay for light that fell only on other people's streets, and several said they would withhold the next year's tax.

The council answered both complaints at its December meeting. The moon schedule was dropped. Instead, Dorn was to look at the sky each evening and light the lamps on any night too cloudy for the moon to show. Four more lamps were ordered, to stand along Mill Row and on the bridge between.

The changes raised the town's kerosene bill, and the council paid it. Dorn kept the job for six years. His notebook, in which he wrote a word or two about the sky every evening, is now kept by the county historical society. Its first entry, for December 14, 1871, reads "Thick. Lit all."

Most birds announce themselves when they fly. A pigeon taking off from a sidewalk claps its wings; even a small songbird makes a soft whir that a person can hear from several feet away. A barn owl flying past at the same distance may make almost no sound a person can detect.

For an owl, that quiet serves two purposes. Many owls hunt at night, and they find much of their prey by sound. In experiments, barn owls have caught mice in rooms too dark for the birds to see them, striking within a few degrees of the place where a mouse rustled through leaves. A bird listening that closely is helped by wings that make little noise of their own. The quiet also gives a mouse less warning.

The quiet comes mostly from the feathers. Along the front edge of each of an owl's outer wing feathers runs a row of stiff, comb-like points. As the wing moves forward, these points appear to break the air flowing over it into smaller swirls, which make less noise than the larger ones a smooth edge would produce. The trailing edges of the feathers end in a soft, ragged fringe instead of a clean line, and the upper surface of the wing is covered with a velvety down that seems to muffle the rustle of feather against feather.

The shape of the wing helps too. Barn owls have large wings for the weight of their bodies, so they can stay aloft while flying slowly and flap less often than a bird with smaller wings. Slower air over the wing makes less sound.

One clue that these features are worth having comes from owls that hunt differently. Several owls in Asia and Africa feed largely on fish, which they snatch from the surface of rivers. A fish underwater is unlikely to hear a bird approaching through the air, and these fish-eating owls lack most of the comb and fringe found on their mouse-hunting relatives.

The soft feathers may also carry a cost. One study found that barn owl feathers let water through more readily than the feathers of some other birds, which may help explain why barn owls are often said to struggle in wet weather.

Engineers, who spend a great deal of effort making machines quieter, have found the owl's solution worth borrowing. Some companies now sell fans whose blades have jagged edges inspired by owl feathers, for buildings where a quieter fan is worth paying for.
